n: Two rival groups, the Pharisees and Sadducees, unite against Jesus. They demand a sign from heaven, hoping to trap or discredit him.

f.g: A priestly, aristocratic party tied to the temple; they rejected the resurrection and oral traditions.

n: Jesus points to weather lore everyone knew: a red evening sky promises good weather.

f.g: Similar to the saying “Red sky at night, sailor’s delight.”

n: A red, overcast morning sky warns of a storm. They read the sky well but miss the obvious signs that the Messiah is among them.
As in chapter 12, the only sign given will be Jonah’s — Jesus’s death and resurrection after three days. Then he leaves them.

f.w: the sign of the prophet Jonas

n: Crossing the lake again, the disciples realize they forgot to bring bread.

f.g: Mark notes they had only one loaf in the boat.

n: Jesus warns them to beware the “leaven” of the Pharisees and Sadducees — a metaphor for something small that spreads and corrupts.

f.g: Yeast; often a symbol of corrupting influence.

n: The disciples take him literally and think he is scolding them for forgetting bread.
Jesus gently rebukes their small faith. Worrying about bread with him in the boat shows they still don’t trust him fully.
He reminds them of feeding the 5,000 with five loaves and the twelve baskets left over.

f.w: the five loaves of the five thousand

n: And the 4,000 fed with seven loaves, with seven baskets left over. Lack of bread is no problem for him.

f.w: the seven loaves of the four thousand

n: Jesus asks how they could miss that he wasn’t talking about literal bread at all.

f.w: I spake it not to you concerning bread

n: Finally they understand: the “leaven” was the false teaching and influence of the religious leaders.
At Caesarea Philippi, far north near Mount Hermon, Jesus asks what people are saying about who he is.

f.g: A city near the headwaters of the Jordan, rebuilt by Herod’s son Philip; home to a shrine of the god Pan.

n: Popular opinion sees him as a great prophet returned — John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, or another.
Then the personal question that every disciple must answer: “But who do you say that I am?”

f.w: But whom say ye that I am?

n: Peter answers boldly: Jesus is the Christ, the promised Messiah, and the Son of the living God.

f.g: Greek Christos = Hebrew Mashiach (Messiah), “the Anointed One.”

f.w: the Son of the living God

n: Jesus blesses Peter and explains that this knowledge came by revelation from the Father, not from human reasoning.

f.w: flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee

n: A play on words: Peter (Petros) means “rock.” Joseph Smith taught that the rock on which Christ builds his Church is revelation, and the powers of hell will not overcome it.

f.g: The power of death and the forces of evil.

n: Jesus promises Peter the keys of the kingdom — the authority to direct God’s work, so that what is sealed on earth is sealed in heaven.
Jesus tells them not to announce publicly that he is the Messiah yet, since many expected a political liberator.
A turning point: Jesus now begins teaching plainly that he must suffer, die in Jerusalem, and rise on the third day.

f.w: From that time forth began Jesus
be raised again the third day

n: Peter, who just confessed Jesus as Messiah, pulls him aside and insists this must never happen. A suffering Messiah didn’t fit his expectations.

f.g: Literally “God be merciful to you” — meaning “God forbid!”

n: Jesus sternly rebukes Peter. Discouraging the Savior from the Atonement echoes Satan’s temptations. Peter is thinking like a man, not like God.

f.g: savourest = have a taste for, are mindful of.

n: To follow Jesus means denying ourselves and taking up our cross. The JST explains this as denying ourselves ungodliness and every worldly lust and keeping his commandments.
Grasping at life on our own terms leads to losing it; giving our life to Christ is how we truly find it.

f.w: lose his life for my sake shall find it

n: Nothing in the world is worth trading for our soul. Its value is beyond any price.

f.w: gain the whole world, and lose his own soul

n: Christ will return in glory with his angels and judge each person according to what they have done.

f.w: reward every man according to his works

n: Some standing there would see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom before dying — perhaps fulfilled days later at the Transfiguration. Latter-day revelation adds that John the Beloved was allowed to remain on earth.
